posts.name: Telmo
posts.cooked:
Updated 18 November after the committee’s question. Changed since 7 November: new sections “Generality” and “Misuse”; the family count (about 30 was out of date, it is over 50); the plan’s weeks 1 to 3 and 5 to 6; the state table; the answers on what exists today and on a source level linter; a section on earlier funding. The plan stays six weeks and USD 1,000.

In my own words

What it solves. Every CKB lock and type has to refuse the same handful of tricks: skim an output, ride a second cell along, swap a dep, reuse a proof. Most teams test that their script works, not that it refuses. ckb-adversary takes one real transaction your script accepts, tries those tricks on it, and tells you which ones got through and who would lose.

Who uses it. Anyone writing or reviewing a CKB script, before deploying: one command on a testnet transaction, or a GitHub Action on every change.

Why me. At LusoCryptoLabs we build on CKB every day: the Cellula names contracts on mainnet, a hosted Fiber LSP on testnet, fixes merged into Fiber. We built this first for our own scripts. In November we replayed an RGB++ lock with it and misjudged what it reported. I want a tool that makes that hard to miss, for every team.

How I work. AI coding tools write a large part of the code. The design is mine: which attacks matter, what counts as a finding, and nothing is accepted until a test fails first, for the right reason.

1. Project Overview

  • Name: ckb-adversary
  • One line: a command line tool that replays a real CKB transaction your script accepts, applies generic attacks to it, and tells you which ones your script accepted and should probably refuse.
  • Type: developer tool (Rust crate and CLI), open source.

2. Team Profile

  • Telmo da Silva (LusoCryptoLabs, Porto): author and maintainer.
  • Background: at LusoCryptoLabs, a small studio in Porto, we build on CKB: the Cellula names and wallet, a hosted Fiber LSP on testnet, and fixes merged into Fiber and CCC. We review public CKB code, read only, with reproduction tests, and a finding with live exposure goes to its owner first, in private.
  • Links: github.com/LusoCryptoLabs, lusocryptolabs.com
  • Contact: hello@lusocryptolabs.com, Discord: tecmeup
  • Earlier Spark project: SoMo Pixel Territory (2025). The technical MVP was delivered and the user testing was not, and the committee reduced the grant from 1,200 to 680 USD. This proposal has no user testing or community work: every deliverable is a tool, a report or a video you can run or watch.
  • Other funding: the DAO grant for Cellula on Fiber (t/11089). It pays for different work. Nothing in this proposal is paid by it.

Recent public work from LusoCryptoLabs on CKB: Rust fixes merged into Fiber: fiber#1707, fiber#1708 and fiber#1715; and a testnet deployment issue reported to Spore, spore-contract#77.

3. Project Background

On August 15, 2026, 16.59M CKB was taken from RGB++ cells with 1,464 forged Bitcoin proofs, and it went unnoticed for 80 days. Per the RGB++ Association, a verification result was checked for an error but not for validity. Changing one byte of the proof and watching the script still accept it would have shown it.

That test, and dozens of others like it, are the same for every lock and type on CKB. Writing them by hand for each script is slow work, so most teams skip them.

Scenario: before deploying a new lock, a team runs ckb-adversary replay on one testnet transaction the lock accepts. For each attack the lock accepted, the report names the attack, the field it touched and who would lose. They fix those before mainnet.

4. Solution

Give it a transaction hash and the code hash of the script under review. It rebuilds the transaction exactly, applies over 50 families of attacks, most of which do not depend on the script (the ones that read a proof or a state cell need a small function from the reviewer), runs each through a copy of the node’s checks, and reports what the script accepted that it should probably refuse: findings, where someone loses, and reviews, where a person decides.

How it differs:

  • ckb-testtool runs your own tests and accepts transactions a node would refuse (no fee, under occupied capacity). This adds the node’s checks.
  • ckb-debugger runs one transaction. It does not invent the attacker’s.
  • Hand-written negative tests cover what the author thought of. These are the cases authors usually miss, the same for every script.

Generality

Why the same attacks fit any script. An attack changes the transaction, not the script’s logic: take one shannon from someone else’s output, add a cell that pays for nothing, move a relative since, swap a cell dep for a look-alike, flip each witness byte the script ignores. The transaction format defines these, so they apply to every lock and type. The verdict is the same for all of them: a copy of the node’s checks decides whether the changed transaction is valid, each script group is then run on its own, and an oracle compares who ends with what.

What a user gives. A transaction hash the script accepted, and the code hash of the script under review. The tool rebuilds the transaction, checks that the script accepts it before any attack, and stops if it does not. It runs the deployed binary, so the language the script was written in does not matter.

Ways to cover more, all optional and all in the library today. The reviewer can declare invariants (supply, one cell per id, immutable content), add a function that signs the changed transaction again (on a testnet the author holds the key, so a signature lock stops hiding the script), and add a function that rebuilds the statement a proof makes. Without them the attacks that need none still run. The funded work puts the command and the report around these, and the example repository shows a signing function and a proof function.

What has run. One harness replays system locks (secp256k1, SPHINCS+), JoyID, xUDT, sUDT, Spore and Cluster (replayed on testnet), CoTA, the Nervos DAO, the Fiber funding and commitment locks, and the Cellula names scripts. On 11 November our own sweep, a test harness driven by private scripts and not a command, ran over 46 indexed mainnet scripts. The same harness ran on every one that had a transaction, with no option set per script. 30 passed the replay checks with no finding. 10 stopped before a result: 5 on witness bytes the script ignores, which need a person to judge and have not been judged yet; 1 on a limit of the harness; 2 where the replay or the node checks refused the honest transaction itself; 1 since fixed in the tool; 1 not yet explained. 4 had no usable transaction, and 2 did not finish within the time limit.

A pass means the honest transaction replayed and no generic attack got through on that one transaction. It is not a statement that the script is safe: for a signature lock every change is refused at the signature. The sweep is our own private run and cannot be rerun from this proposal. The coverage report in week 6 can be rerun line by line.

What is not general, today.

  • A lock that checks a signature refuses every change, so a bug behind it is hidden. Without a signing function the tool cannot sign for a stranger’s key. Signed transactions are the weakest case.
  • Scripts that verify a proof or read a state cell need a small function from the reviewer to rebuild the statement. Without it only the attacks that need none run.
  • One transaction is one code path. The report says which path each took, and the data hash of the binary it ran against.
  • The replay uses today’s rules and a cycle cap, not the rules at the time of the transaction.
  • Whether a reported finding is real is the author’s call, as with any warning. The report names the attack and the field, so the check is short.

What the funded work changes. The 10 scripts that stopped in November become part of the test list: each is replayed again, each ignored byte is judged, and the replay is fixed in the tool with a test or the script is listed as out of reach with the reason. The coverage report states how many of the scripts tested ran end to end with only a transaction hash and a code hash.

Misuse

It is meant for the people who write or review a script, run on their own script. It reads public chain data and sends no transaction. It runs changed copies of a transaction that is already on chain, in a local copy of the node’s checks, so a changed copy of a spent transaction cannot be broadcast. It holds no keys. A report names the attack, the field and who would lose, and never contains a transaction ready to send.

A finding in an unsigned script can still be used without anyone’s key, which is why a finding goes to the owner first, in private. Thirty days after the owner is told is the earliest I publish, not a fixed rule: I follow the owner’s own policy if it has one, and I wait longer while a fix that needs a migration is under way. If I cannot reach an owner I try two channels and ask Nervos security first.

What we have said in public so far concerned cases with no live exposure, a fix already public, a documentation request or a testnet deployment: omnilock#12, a comment on ckb-system-scripts#106, ckb-proxy-locks#8 and spore-contract#77. Anything with live exposure goes to its owner first. The attacks are known classes and the script code is already public on chain, so the tool gives an attacker little that they could not already do. Fuzzers and static analysers are shared the same way.

5. Technical Approach

  • Stack: Rust, on ckb-testtool and CKB’s own verifiers. Node checks adapted from iCKB’s VerifyRealistic (MIT). Output in English.
  • A verdict: rebuild the honest transaction and check its hash against the chain; apply each attack; drop mutants the node itself would refuse; run each script group on its own; an oracle flags a loss for someone other than the attacker, a cell riding free, or a broken stated rule; every verdict is compared with a stored file in CI.
  • Hardest part: a witness byte the script ignores is either harmless (a Bitcoin segwit signature) or the bug (a proof never checked). The report maps each ignored byte to its field and only allows fields provably outside every check.

6. To-Do List

  1. Week 1: open the repository under MIT. A replay command that fetches a transaction by hash from a public RPC (mainnet or testnet, set with --rpc), captures its cell deps as they were, and checks the rebuilt hash. README with a five-minute quick start.
  2. Week 2: a report as a table and as JSON, with each witness byte the script ignores mapped to the field it belongs to. A GitHub Action and an example repository with a deliberately vulnerable script that fails CI, and its fixed version that passes, with a signing function and a proof function as examples, and a control where the script is swapped for one that accepts everything and must report findings. Milestone: v0.1 released.
  3. Week 3: publish the list of scripts to test: the most used locks and types on mainnet by CKB held in live cells, from a public indexer (about 15). Collect one honest transaction for each and run. Add the 10 scripts that stopped in November: replay each again, judge each ignored byte, and fix the replay in the tool with a test or explain why it is out of reach. The 4 without a transaction and the 2 that did not finish are listed with the reason. The owners of the scripts on the list are told before it is published.
  4. Week 4: check every accepted attack by hand. A real finding goes to week 5. Noise becomes a fix in the tool, with a test, so it does not come back.
  5. Week 5: report real findings privately to each owner. Nothing is published before the disclosure rule in Misuse allows it. Write the coverage table.
  6. Week 6: final report, which states how many of the scripts tested ran end to end with no per script input, a five-minute demo video, docs. Milestone: v0.2 released.

I post a short update in this thread every week, and if I am away for more than a week I say so that week.

7. Required Funding and Breakdown

Total: $1,000, paid in CKB. All technical work; no community or marketing spend. It is a fixed sum for the milestones, not an hourly rate. If the committee prefers a lower sum, I accept it and drop, in this order: the demo video, the polish of the Action, fewer scripts. Spark pays only for the public work listed here. The hosted scan page and paid reviews we run separately are not funded by Spark.

Weeks Work USD
1 to 2 Public release, replay with RPC fetch, field-mapped report, GitHub Action and example 400
3 to 4 Run on about 15 mainnet scripts and the 10 that stopped in November (some overlap), check every accepted attack, fix noise in the tool 400
5 to 6 Private reports to owners, coverage report, demo video, docs 200

8. Deliverables and How to Verify

A. Deliverables

Deliverable Done when
Public repository (MIT), CI green, tags v0.1 and v0.2 The tags exist and CI passes on them
ckb-adversary replay --network <mainnet or testnet> --tx <hash> --code-hash <hash> It runs on any transaction marked ran in the report, on Linux or WSL with a recent stable Rust and a C compiler
GitHub Action and example repository The vulnerable example’s CI fails and names the attack; the fixed one passes
Coverage report Lists each script, the transaction used, the data hash of the binary it ran against, the families run and the verdict counts; findings shown only as the disclosure rule in Misuse allows
Demo video, five minutes Public link

B. How to Verify, without reading the code

  1. Install from the repository link in the v0.1 release notes: cargo install --git <repository> --tag v0.1.
  2. Run it on a plain secp256k1 transfer from the report. Expected: every attack refused, 0 findings. This is a control only: a signature lock refuses every change.
  3. Open the example repository’s CI. Expected: the vulnerable script’s run fails and names the attack and who would lose; the fixed script’s run passes; the script swapped for one that accepts everything reports findings.
  4. Pick any line marked ran in the coverage report and run the command printed beside it. Expected: the same summary line (mutants, findings, reviews). The 11 November sweep is a private run and is not part of what you verify.

Environment: Linux or WSL, a recent stable Rust and a C compiler, internet for the public RPC. No node needed. Most checks take under two minutes; a lock with large proofs can take longer.

9. Current State vs. Funded Work

Today (private prototype, started November 2026) Funded by Spark
Code Rust library: over 50 attack families, the node’s checks, per-group verification, verdict files Public under MIT, versioned releases
Input Transactions picked and replayed by our own sweep tooling, which stays private replay fetches a transaction by hash and rebuilds it with its deps as they were
Output Test results read by the author A table and JSON report, each ignored witness byte mapped to its field
Users Us, and owners who ask for a scan of their own script on a page we run, where only the holder of the deploy key sees the result. Nobody else can run the engine today. Any team, from the command line or a GitHub Action, with an example to copy
Coverage Scripts with known bugs written to test it, honest replays of 9 deployed scripts (secp256k1, JoyID, xUDT, sUDT, Spore and Cluster on testnet, CoTA, RGB++, BTC time lock), and a private sweep over 46 indexed mainnet scripts on 11 November (30 passed, 10 stopped before a result, 4 without a transaction, 2 unfinished) About 15 of the most used mainnet scripts by CKB held, every accepted attack checked by hand, owners told in private, a public coverage report

10. CKB Alignment

The attacks are built on what is specific to the Cell Model: lock and type script groups, relative and absolute since and its metrics, header deps, cell deps and dep groups, hash_type (data, data1, data2, type), occupied capacity, type id, and xUDT owner mode. The node checks come from CKB’s own verifiers. It does not use Fiber, Spore or JoyID features itself. It is a general tool for anyone who writes or reviews a CKB script, and it runs against those scripts like any other.

Questions we expect

How do you use AI? AI coding tools write a large part of the code, as they now do for many teams. What we keep in our hands is what decides whether the tool is right: which attacks matter, what counts as a finding, and a test that must fail before any fix is accepted.

It already exists, so why fund it? What exists works for us: test seeds built by hand, and a page where an owner can scan their own script and only they see the result. Spark pays for neither. The money pays for the open tool anyone can run on their own scripts: fetching any transaction by hash, a report a stranger can read, a GitHub Action, and a coverage report on about 15 mainnet scripts.

How is this different from a source level linter? A linter reads source and flags patterns. This runs the deployed binary on a real transaction, so it needs no source, and everything it reports is something the binary accepted. It cannot say why, and it reaches less on signature locks. A team can use both.

What if it finds a hole in a live contract? The owner hears first, in private. Nothing is published before the disclosure rule in Misuse allows it.

Won’t it flood teams with false alarms? A mutant the node itself would refuse is never reported, every verdict is checked by hand during the six weeks, and every false alarm we find becomes a fix in the tool with a test.

Which scripts will you run it on? The most used locks and types on mainnet by CKB held in live cells, about 15, published in week 3 with the transaction used for each.

What happens after Spark? Nothing is hosted, so there is nothing to keep running. Every attack family we add to the engine is released with its test. I keep it working with new CKB releases and review pull requests for six months, and say in this thread if I stop. If teams adopt it, a larger proposal can come later, based on real use.

posts.name: 行天春彦
posts.cooked:
Hi @T_Silva,

Thank you for your continued interest in the Spark Program and for submitting the ckb-adversary proposal.

After review by the Spark Program committee, your proposal’s status is Pending. This is not a rejection, but an invitation to revise your proposal.

The committee recognizes the value of the project concept: a general-purpose attack replay tool for CKB scripts could make a meaningful contribution to developers’ security practices, particularly in light of RGB++ events.

Generality and Ease of Use Across a Broader Ecosystem: The committee is curious because security tools of this kind are typically developed specifically for individual projects. How does ckb-adversary achieve greater generality so that other projects can use it for security scans? And what technical approaches enable it to cover more general use cases, allowing more applications and smart contracts to use the tool?

Please revise and resubmit your proposal based on this feedback. We’ll arrange another review as soon as possible.

Best regards
xingtian
On behalf of the Spark Program Committee

posts.name: Telmo
posts.cooked:
Thank you, @xingtianchunyan. Short answer: the attacks change fields every transaction has (outputs, since, witnesses, cell deps, header deps, hash type, args), not the script’s logic, so the same attacks run on any lock or type. You give it a transaction the script accepted and its code hash, and it runs the deployed binary, so the language of the script does not matter.

Measured on 11 November with our own private harness: a real transaction picked for 42 of 46 mainnet targets (4 had none), no option set per script. 30 passed the replay checks, which is not a statement that they are safe. 16 did not run end to end, and I list why in the proposal. Signature locks and scripts that check proofs are the weak spots, and I say so there.

I edited the proposal. The changes are listed at its top. The plan stays six weeks and USD 1,000.

posts.name: 行天春彦
posts.cooked:
Hi @T_Silva,

Thank you for taking the time to revise the proposal based on our earlier feedback.

The committee has completed its review and has determined that the proposal does not fall within the scope of the Spark Program. Therefore, we regret to inform you that the proposal has been rejected.

Thank you very much for all the hard work your team has put in. Keep building, and feel free to reach out anytime!

Best,
xingtian
On behalf of the Spark Program Committee
